author: blu
body: The AgentProtocol defines agent identity (Ed25519 public key), capability grants with direction and scope, and the message types exchanged over the trust network. Seven cover the capability and control vocabulary; two more -- Annotate and Verdict -- carry knowledge about code as opaque payload bytes, letting Works own the encoding while keeping kind dispatch at the protocol layer.

author: blu
body: The last two -- Annotate and Verdict -- carry knowledge about code: a SignedAnnotation published by an author, and a Verdict signed by a reviewer responding to one. They live at the protocol layer alongside the capability messages so the trust filter can dispatch on kind, but their payloads cross the layer boundary as opaque bytes -- the Works layer (RepoProtocol) owns the encoding of ProposalPayload and Verdict.

author: blu
body: The last two -- SyncOffer and SyncReply -- carry a fact-store reconciliation over the same wire. An offer names the hashes a peer holds; a reply carries the facts the offering peer was missing. Both bodies are opaque payload bytes whose encoding belongs to the FactSync layer, exactly as Annotate and Verdict defer to Works. Content addressing makes the exchange conflict-free: a hash is present or it is not, and merging in either direction converges.

author: blu
body: An empty payload is the honest answer for "I do not have it". It is not an error: a peer that does not hold a work is the normal case, and the asker's job is to try the next peer. Neither message is signed, and that is deliberate -- the reply is answerable by its own content. The asker hashes what comes back and checks it against the hash it asked for, so a lying peer is caught by the addressing rather than by trusting the peer. That is the same reason the gate can let the transport be untrusted.

author: blu
body: The payload is Text, where the sync payloads are bytes, and that is not inconsistency. A work's wire form IS text -- it is what `sdw-encode` produces and what the compiler's own reader decodes -- and content addressing here is over CCE bytes by decision, so handing the text across and letting the frame encode it keeps one representation rather than three. An empty payload is "not here".

author: blu
body: Ask who holds a work, rather than asking for the work. A quotation names a digest and nothing else, so an asker that has not already been introduced to a holder has no way to turn that digest into an address. This is the verb that turns it into one.

author: blu
body: The reply carries addresses and no content. That is the whole reason it is a separate verb from WorkRequest: an address cannot be checked, so it is never believed -- it is only used, by fetching from it and hashing what comes back. The registry therefore does not need to hold, or ever have held, the work it points at, and cannot be made responsible for the honesty of a peer it names.

author: blu
body: `peers` is a space-separated list of `host:port`, empty when the registry knows nobody who holds the digest. Empty is the ordinary answer and not an error, exactly as an empty work payload is: a registry that has not been told about a holder simply has not been told.

author: blu
body: Neither message is signed, for the same reason the work pair is not. A signed rumour is still a rumour, and the check that actually protects the asker happens after the fetch, against the content.

author: blu
body: A peer announcing what it holds. `address` is where the peer can be reached (`host:port`), and `hashes` is a space-separated list of the digests it is offering at that address. The reply is an acknowledgement carrying the count the registry recorded, so a peer can tell a registry that took its announcement from one that never heard it.

author: blu
body: The peer states its OWN address rather than the registry inferring it from the connection, because the address a registry would infer is the one the peer dialled from, and that is not the address anyone else reaches it on.

author: blu
body: The scaling ceiling is real and is not solved here: a peer holding the whole compiler announces thousands of digests in one message. When that bites, the answer is a compact summary (`Foreword chapter BloomFilter` / `ElasticBloom`) rather than a longer list, and a probabilistic summary is safe precisely because the fetch path already tolerates a miss on a named peer.
